procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Calcutta (exercise of its original jurisdiction)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the Calcutta High Court dated February 6, 1970 in Criminal Appeal No. 5 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a petition of appeal under s. 41 lA, Cr. P.C., on September 7, 1964, challenging his conviction and the sentences imposed on him. The High Court, by its judgment dated September 19, 1967 in Criminal Appeal No. 5 of 1964, confirmed the conviction and sentences imposed on the appellant. The appellant sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against the judgment of the High Court on October 21, 1967, and the same was refused on January 8, 1968. After remand from the Supreme Court, the High Court issued a judgment and order dated February 6, 1970.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant initially sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against the High Court's judgment of October 21, 1967, which was refused. He then obtained special leave and filed an appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 190 of 1968). The Supreme Court, on April 30, 1969, set aside the High Court's judgment and order of September 19, 1967, and remanded the appeal to the High Court for fresh disposal. The current appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 137 of 1970) is before the Supreme Court again, this time limited to the question of sentence only.

directions: remanded the appeal to the High Court for fresh disposal and hearing in accordance with law and in the light of the observations contained in this Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed by the High Court was appropriate.

facts: The appellant was convicted of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death by the High Court.
The High Court acknowledged that there had been a long delay in hearing the appeal but did not consider it a sufficient reason to reduce the death sentence.
By the time the Supreme Court heard the case, the appellant had been under the fear of a death sentence for more than six years.
The Supreme Court noted this period must have caused the appellant "unimaginable mental agony".
law: Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) prescribes two alternative sentences for murder: the death penalty or imprisonment for life.

An "inordinate delay" in the disposal of an appeal by the High Court is a relevant factor for the court to take into consideration when deciding whether to impose the lesser sentence (imprisonment for life).
application: The Supreme Court found that the more than six-year delay in the final disposal of the appellant's case was "extremely excessive."
The Court reasoned that this excessive delay, by itself, was a sufficient ground for imposing the lesser sentence of life imprisonment.
It concluded that it would be "inhuman" to make the appellant suffer further while waiting for the government to decide on a mercy petition.
Therefore, the Court determined that the case was a fit one for awarding the lesser sentence due to the mental agony caused by the prolonged legal process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appeal, set aside the High Court's order awarding the death sentence, and instead imposed a sentence of imprisonment for life. It held that the death sentence was inappropriate given the inordinate delay in the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in leaving the matter of the sentence to the State Government.

facts: The appellant was under the fear of a death sentence for over six years, which the Supreme Court noted must have caused "unimaginable mental agony."

The High Court acknowledged the "inordinate delay" in the case but, citing the precedent of *Nawab Singh v. The State of Uttar Pradesh*, left the decision of whether to reduce the sentence to the State Government.
The appellant's counsel argued that the matter of the sentence should not have been left to the State Government.
law: The Supreme Court established that under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, which prescribes either a death sentence or life imprisonment, an "inordinate delay" in the disposal of an appeal is a relevant factor for the court to consider when imposing the lesser sentence.

While acknowledging the precedent that commuting a sentence due to delay is primarily a matter for the government, the Court held that in cases of "extremely excessive delay," it is a fit matter for the court itself to decide.
application: The Court found that the more than six-year delay in this case was "extremely excessive" and, by itself, was a sufficient reason to impose the lesser sentence of life imprisonment.
The Court reasoned that it would be "inhuman" to make the appellant continue to suffer while waiting for the government to decide the matter on a mercy petition.
Therefore, the Court determined that this was a "fit case for awarding the lesser sentence instead of leaving it to the Government to decide the matter."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred. It held that due to the excessive delay, the court itself should have commuted the sentence. The Supreme Court accepted the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and reduced the appellant's death sentence to life imprisonment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed by the High Court was appropriate.
appellant_arguments: The sentence of death should be reduced to rigorous imprisonment for life on account of the long delay that had taken place in hearing the appeal and the consequent mental suffering undergone by the condemned prisoner.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not mentioned in the provided text. However, they would have supported the High Court's initial finding that the murder was premeditated and cold-blooded, making it a fit case for capital punishment, and that delay was not a sufficient ground for commutation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in leaving the matter of the sentence to the State Government.
appellant_arguments: The matter of the sentence should not have been left to the State Government.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not mentioned in the provided text.

cases.case_name: Nawab Singh v. The State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: Regarding the legal propriety of leaving a matter to be decided by the State Government.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An inordinate delay in the execution of a death sentence is not a rule of law that necessitates its commutation by a court; this consideration is primarily a matter for the government. If a court does exercise discretion in such a matter, it must take all other facts of the case into consideration.
obiter: Though the conviction was for an offence under section 302 read with section 149, I.P.C., curiously they were sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment, and none of them challenged their conviction in appeals.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When there has been inordinate delay in the disposal of the appeal by the High Court, it is a relevant factor for the High Court to take into consideration for imposing the lesser sentence. In view of the excessive delay, it is a fit case for awarding the lesser sentence instead of leaving it to the Government to decide the matter on a mercy petition.
legal_tests_applied: Whether there has been an inordinate delay in the disposal of the appeal, which is a relevant factor for the High Court to take into consideration for imposing the lesser of two alternate sentences prescribed by law (death or imprisonment for life under Section 302, I.P.C.).
policy_considerations: An appellant being under the fear of a sentence of death for a prolonged period (6 years in this case) must have caused unimaginable mental agony, which is a factor in sentencing.

The choice between prescribed alternate sentences is a judicial function; it is not appropriate for a court to leave the matter of commuting a sentence due to delay to the discretion of the State Government on a mercy petition.
